issues.legal_issue: A sublease executed before an amendment but expressly commencing after the amendment’s commencement date does not make the lessee a subtenant on the amendment’s commencement date.
material_facts: The sublease was executed on 5 June 1947 and registered on 22 June 1947.
It expressly provided that the tenancy would commence on 1 July 1947.
The amendment introducing section 295A came into force on 14 June 1947.
issues.conclusion: Section 295A did not apply because the lessees were not subtenants on 14 June 1947.
issues.legal_principle: Section 295A of the U.P. Tenancy Act, 1939 applied to a person who was a subtenant on the amendment’s commencement date. Under section 55(1), delivery of a lease and counterpart does not itself make the tenancy commence on the delivery date; the lease rights arise according to the lease’s terms. The Court also referred to section 56, which required registration for a lease from year to year or for more than one year.

predicates.sublease_commences_after_amendment_start: The sublease provides that the tenancy begins after the relevant amendment has come into force.
predicates.subtenant_status_depends_on_sublease: The claimed status as a subtenant on the amendment’s commencement date depends on that sublease.

issues.definition: When a sublease begins only after the amendment has come into force, a status dependent on that sublease is not held on the amendment’s commencement date.

issues.legal_issue: An agricultural sublease that specifies annual rent but no duration is not treated as a five-year lease merely because the tenant could lawfully sublet for up to five years.
material_facts: The sublease reserved annual rent but stated no term.
The tenant’s authority to sublet was limited to a maximum period of five years.
No conduct of the parties showed that they intended the sublease to last five years.
The lessees did not contend that the sublease was permanent, which would have made it invalid in their case.
issues.conclusion: The sublease was from year to year, not for a fixed term of five years.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the principle stated in Janaki Nath Roy v. Dina Nath Kundu that an indefinite lease of this kind is either permanent or from year to year, with no intermediate interpretation. It referred to Surendra Kumar Sen Chaudhury v. Chandratara Nath for the use of the parties’ conduct where lease terms are ambiguous, and distinguished Mohd. Sher Khan v. Special Manager, Court of Wards, which did not establish that an unspecified term should be treated as five years.

rule.if: agricultural_sublease and annual_rent_reserved and duration_omitted and no_conduct_supports_five_year_term and permanent_term_not_claimed

predicates.agricultural_sublease: The parties made a sublease of agricultural land.
predicates.annual_rent_reserved: The sublease reserved rent payable annually.
predicates.duration_omitted: The sublease did not state how long it would last.
predicates.no_conduct_supports_five_year_term: The parties’ conduct did not show that they intended the sublease to last five years.
predicates.permanent_term_not_claimed: The tenant did not claim that the sublease was permanent.

issues.definition: An agricultural sublease with annual rent and no stated duration is treated as from year to year when the parties’ conduct does not show a five-year term and a permanent term is not claimed.

issues.legal_issue: A subtenant’s statutory right to remain after the chief tenant’s interest ends lasts only for the remainder of the sublease term or the statutory maximum, whichever is shorter, and possession after that period does not preserve the status required for the claimed landholding classification.
material_facts: The chief tenant surrendered his tenancy on 15 January 1951, extinguishing the subtenants’ interests under the original sublease.
The sublease was from year to year, and the subtenants’ current term ran only until 30 June 1951.
The subtenants remained in possession after 30 June 1951.
The relevant date for the claimed landholding classification was 30 June 1952.
issues.conclusion: The statutory continuation right ended on 30 June 1951. Possession after that date was not in the capacity of a protected subtenant, so the land was not held in the capacity required for the claimed classification.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 47(1) and 47(4) of the U.P. Tenancy Act, 1939 provide that extinction of the chief tenant’s interest extinguishes the subtenant’s interest, but a valid sublease may give the subtenant a new, limited right to remain for the remainder of its term or five years, whichever is shorter. Section 19(vii) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950 required the land to be held on the relevant date by a subtenant referred to in section 47(4). The Court applied the periodic-tenancy reasoning in Utility Articles Manufacturing Co. v. Raja Bahadur Motilal Bombay Mills Ltd. and Queen’s Club Gardens Estate Ltd. v. Bignell, and distinguished Ram Dular Singh v. Babu Sukhu Ram: no eviction is required to end a right that the statute itself grants only for a limited period.

rule.if: claim_for_landholding_status_as_protected_subtenant and chief_tenant_interest_ended and valid_sublease_existed_at_termination and remaining_sublease_term_expired_before_relevant_status_date and subtenant_remained_in_possession_after_expiry

predicates.claim_for_landholding_status_as_protecte: A party claims a landholding classification on the basis of being a protected subtenant on the relevant status date.
predicates.chief_tenant_interest_ended: The chief tenant’s interest ended by surrender or another event covered by the governing rule.
predicates.valid_sublease_existed_at_termination: A valid sublease was in existence when the chief tenant’s interest ended.
predicates.remaining_sublease_term_expired_before_r: The remaining term of the sublease ended before the date on which the claimed status had to exist.
predicates.subtenant_remained_in_possession_after_e: The subtenant continued in possession after the remaining sublease term ended.

issues.definition: When a party claims status as a protected subtenant but the remaining term ended before the relevant date, continued possession after expiry does not establish that status on that date.
